Extremely slow scaling of minimal Hamming distance in quantum sampling data

P. S. Golubev Affiliation: Theoretical Physics and Applied Mathematics Department, Ural Federal University, Ekaterinburg 620002, Russia    I. A. Iakovlev Affiliation: Theoretical Physics and Applied Mathematics Department, Ural Federal University, Ekaterinburg 620002, Russia Affiliation: Russian Quantum Center, Skolkovo, Moscow 121205, Russia    V. V. Mazurenko Affiliation: Theoretical Physics and Applied Mathematics Department, Ural Federal University, Ekaterinburg 620002, Russia Affiliation: Russian Quantum Center, Skolkovo, Moscow 121205, Russia
Abstract

Quantum data can be obtained from a diverse range of sources, including direct measurements from noisy quantum processors, cold-atom simulators, and classical approximations such as variational neural-network states. However, our ability to characterize these systems is fundamentally limited, as the available measurement data are often sparse compared to the exponentially large Hilbert space of the system. To address this, we propose using the expected minimal Hamming distance calculated for a set of unique bitstrings as a robust metric revealing a distinct power-law behaviour. Crucially, we have established a direct connection between the empirical power-law parameters and the intrinsic dimension of the quantum measurement outcomes. Through various examples of real experiments and simulations, we show that the power-law parameters reliably characterize the underlying geometric structure of measurement outcomes and identify quantum phase transitions from limited quantum information, without the need for accumulating extensive statistics or explicitly calculating physical observables. This enables the analysis of completely different quantum experiments within a single framework. Furthermore, we demonstrate the versatility of our approach on classical high-dimensional data, showing that the power-law parameters can successfully discriminate different classes of handwritten digits from the MNIST dataset.

I Introduction

Quantum state measurement is an integral part of any quantum experiment, including quantum computing, where the final wave function encodes a solution of a problem. The resulting basis states, represented as bitstrings (for instance, ’01000..1’, ’11010..1’), provide only limited information regarding the underlying quantum state, as they are typically few in number compared to the dimensionality of the Hilbert space. This makes extracting the maximum amount of useful information from quantum measurements a nontrivial problem that lacks a universal solution. Numerous measurement-based approaches for characterizing quantum states developed to date mainly focus on estimating standard inter-qubit correlation functions and entropies of different types [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. Alternative approaches [6, 7, 8, 9, 10] treat bit-string arrays as datasets, revealing patterns and quantifying correlations between different samples, effectively abstracting away the quantum origin of the input. Here, various metrics from data science can be applied, and subsequently leveraged as hash functions for the underlying quantum states, facilitating their efficient discrimination.

A primary procedure in processing bit-string arrays for some high-level algorithms mentioned above is the calculation of the Hamming distance [11], which quantifies the number of bits by which two samples differ. For instance, within the wave-function network approaches [12, 13, 14, 15, 16] the minimal Hamming distance averaged over a bit-string array determines the structure of the graph subsequently used for analysis of the quantum state. In certain situations, the Hamming distance on its own facilitates the solution of a problem where error correction [17] and discrimination of non-trivial non-equilibrium quantum states [18, 19] serve as prominent examples. While the Hamming distance metric is extensively applied in quantum computing, its behavior is still poorly understood.

In this work, we characterize state spaces of notable quantum states at the level of projective measurements and reveal a previously unreported feature of the Hamming distance. Namely, for a given wave function, the minimum Hamming distance calculated with moderate sets of unique bitstrings follows a power-law scaling relative to the set size. This scaling behavior reveals the connectivity within the state space and, as we demonstrate from first-principles, is related to the fundamental concept of intrinsic dimension. The corresponding power-law parameters serve as the effective descriptors of the quantum state and enable an efficient state discrimination of large-scale wave functions with a limited number of measurements. In turn, the analysis of the antiferromagnetic J1−J2J_{1}-J_{2} model solutions obtained with the attention-based vision transformer wave function facilitates detecting phase boundaries and estimating accuracy of the neural network approach at different points of the phase space. As an example of non-equilibrium problem we consider the quench dynamics of spin-glass systems simulated on D-Wave quantum processors. Furthermore, a real-world problem that is discrimination of the MNIST digits by their intrinsic dimensions can be likewise solved with our approach.

II Method

To characterize an NN-qubit quantum system described by a wavefunction |Ψ⟩\ket{\Psi}, one performs a series of projective measurements in a specific basis. From these measurements, we collect a total of NbmaxN_{b}^{\text{max}} unique bitstrings, where the ii-th configuration is represented as 𝐱i={xik}k=1,…,N{\bf x}_{i}=\{x_{i}^{k}\}_{k=1,\dots,N} with xik∈{0,1}x_{i}^{k}\in\{0,1\}. Depending on the particular source of measurement data, this total count can vary from 10310^{3} for the D-Wave quantum annealer to 10610^{6} for the Google Sycamore device. Since each sample in this preprocessed record is unique, the probabilities of individual basis states and related frequency-dependent quantities cannot be extracted directly from the data.

As the next step, we randomly subsample NbN_{b} configurations from the entire set of NbmaxN_{b}^{\text{max}} unique outcomes and calculate the mutual Hamming distances between them, d⁡(𝐱i,𝐱j)=∑k=1N|xik−xjk|d({\bf x}_{i},{\bf x}_{j})=\sum_{k=1}^{N}|x^{k}_{i}-x^{k}_{j}|, where i,j=1,…,Nbi,j=1,\dots,N_{b} and i≠ji\neq j. For each bitstring within this subsample, we determine the distance to its first nearest neighbor.

To ensure statistical robustness and eliminate sample-dependent fluctuations, we repeat this generation process to construct several independent datasets of size NbN_{b}. We compute the mean minimal Hamming distance for each dataset and subsequently perform an ensemble average over the resulting values. In this way, we define the expected nearest-neighbor distance function as follows:

r¯1​(Nb)=⟨1Nb​∑i=1Nbminj≠i⁡d⁡(𝐱i,𝐱j)⟩,\bar{r}_{1}(N_{b})=\left\langle\frac{1}{N_{b}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{b}}\min_{j\neq i}d({\bf x}_{i},{\bf x}_{j})\right\rangle, (1)

where ⟨…⟩\langle\dots\rangle denotes the ensemble average evaluated over the generated random realizations of the size-NbN_{b} datasets.

Usually, the average minimum distance r¯1\bar{r}_{1} calculated at a given NbN_{b} is to play a supporting role being used as the cutoff radius when constructing wave function networks [12, 15, 16]. Here we are going to show that the r¯1​(Nb)\bar{r}_{1}(N_{b}) function provides enough information for identification and discrimination of quantum states of different complexity, finding phase boundaries as well as solving other problems.

Fig. 1 displays the r¯1​(Nb)\bar{r}_{1}(N_{b}) dependencies in a log-log scale for several notable large-scale quantum states, for which measurement data are either publicly available from real quantum devices or can be generated on classical computers. Despite the different origin of underlying quantum data, the resulting Hamming functions calculated with measurements in the σz\sigma^{z} basis reveal similar characteristic patterns. Namely, a rapid non-linear decrease with large standard deviations at small values of NbN_{b} is replaced by almost linear behaviour with a slope specific to each wave function. The linear part of the r¯1​(Nb)\bar{r}_{1}(N_{b}) function in the log-log scale can be fitted with

r¯1​(Nb)=A​Nb−α.\displaystyle\bar{r}_{1}(N_{b})=AN_{b}^{-\alpha}. (2)

This motivates using the power-law parameters AA and α\alpha as basis-dependent geometric descriptors to characterize the underlying structure of the sampled bitstrings in a computational basis. While the coefficient AA in Eq. (2) corresponds to the value of r¯1​(Nb)\bar{r}_{1}(N_{b}) at Nb=1N_{b}=1, the minimal number of bitstrings for which the Hamming distance function can be defined is two. Nevertheless, the coefficient AA demonstrates a high sensitivity to variations of a given quantum state, which is particularly useful for efficient state discrimination and can be formally obtained via the Nb→1N_{b}\rightarrow 1 extrapolation of r¯1​(Nb)\bar{r}_{1}(N_{b}). In turn, the exponent α\alpha determines the scaling rate of finding the nearest neighbors in the state space as the sample set increases, which turns out to be extremely slow, with α∈[0.1,0.35]\alpha\in[0.1,0.35] for the quantum states we consider in this work. In Appendix A, we present the additional details regarding the role of bit-string repetitions and the selection of fitting windows.

To establish a physical interpretation of the empirical power-law parameters AA and α\alpha, we have reviewed the foundational literature dedicated to nearest-neighbor statistics across various scientific domains. Remarkably, the theoretical roots of our approach date back to 1909 with the pioneering work by Paul Hertz [23], who first derived the exact nearest-neighbor distance distribution to characterize the spatial layout of molecules in an ideal gas. While Hertz originally focused on three-dimensional physical systems, in 1954 this theoretical framework was adapted by biologists [24] to evaluate the spatial dispersion of plant populations on a two-dimensional plane, and was eventually generalized to arbitrary dd-dimensional space by Clark and Evans [25] in 1979. More specifically, for a random uniform dispersion of independent points in a dd-dimensional space, the mathematical expectation of the distance to the first nearest neighbor in an ideal gas system (r¯1(gas)\bar{r}_{1}^{\text{(gas)}}) is given by:

r¯1(gas)=[Γ⁡(d2+1)]1/d​Γ​(1d+1)π​ρ−1d,\bar{r}_{1}^{\text{(gas)}}=\frac{[\Gamma(\frac{d}{2}+1)]^{1/d}\Gamma(\frac{1}{d}+1)}{\sqrt{\pi}}\rho^{-\frac{1}{d}}, (3)

where Γ⁡(⋅)\Gamma(\cdot) is the Euler Gamma function. Here, ρ\rho is the uniform spatial density of the gas [23] or plants [25].

Eq. (3) establishes a direct connection between the nearest-neighbor distance and the embedding system’s dimension. These ideas were later found to be extremely useful for discovering low-dimensional manifold representations of high-dimensional data [26, 27]. In particular, Pettis et al. [26] considered a dataset, {𝐱1,𝐱2,…,𝐱n}\{{\bf x}_{1},{\bf x}_{2},\dots,{\bf x}_{n}\} of nn samples and derived the following expression for the average nearest-neighbour distance

r¯1(data)≈Cgeom​(1n​∑i=1n[p⁡(𝐱i)]−1d)​n−1d,\bar{r}_{1}^{\text{(data)}}\approx C_{\rm geom}(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}[p({\bf x}_{i})]^{-\frac{1}{d}})n^{-\frac{1}{d}}, (4)

where Cgeom=[Γ⁡(d2+1)]1/d​Γ​(1d+1)πC_{\rm geom}=\frac{[\Gamma(\frac{d}{2}+1)]^{1/d}\Gamma(\frac{1}{d}+1)}{\sqrt{\pi}} and dd is the intrinsic dimension of the underlying manifold. p⁡(𝐱i)p({\bf x}_{i}) represents the local probability density of the generated data at the sample 𝐱i{\bf x}_{i}. For the first nearest neighbor, the local probability density at the sample 𝐱i{\bf x}_{i} is defined as p⁡(𝐱i)=1/nV⁡(𝐱i)p({\bf x}_{i})=\frac{1/n}{V({\bf x}_{i})}, where the numerator 1/n1/n represents the elementary probability weight assigned to a single sample within the total dataset of size nn, and V⁡(𝐱i)=Vd​[r1​(𝐱i)]dV({\bf x}_{i})=V_{d}[r_{1}({\bf x}_{i})]^{d} is the volume of the local hypersphere with Vd=πd/2​[Γ⁡(d/2+1)]−1V_{d}=\pi^{d/2}[\Gamma(d/2+1)]^{-1} being the volume of a unit dd-ball. In this consideration, the probability density p⁡(𝐱i)p({\bf x}_{i}) is assumed to be approximately constant within the local hypersphere centered at 𝐱i{\bf x}_{i} that encompasses its first nearest neighbor.

To apply Eq. (4) to our system, we note that quantum computational outcomes are naturally represented as binary configurations, meaning that all distance calculations are performed strictly within the discrete space {0,1}N\{0,1\}^{N} using the L1L_{1} norm. Taking n=Nbn=N_{b}, this spatial framework can be directly mapped onto our empirical power-law relation given in Eq. (2). This direct mapping yields a clear interpretation of our empirical parameters. The scaling exponent α\alpha can be straightforwardly interpreted as the inverse effective intrinsic dimension of the set of quantum measurement results obtained in a basis, namely deff=α−1d_{\rm eff}=\alpha^{-1}. For instance, a higher value of α\alpha indicates a lower effective dimension, signaling that the measurement outcomes belong to a compact subspace within the overall state space. We examine these conclusions about the intrinsic dimension by using synthetic datasets in the next section.

Simultaneously, the coefficient AA is functionally linked to the averaged inverse probability density of the data, A∼1Nb​∑i=1Nb[p⁡(𝐱i)]−1dA\sim\frac{1}{N_{b}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{b}}[p({\bf x}_{i})]^{-\frac{1}{d}}. This means that the samples with the smallest p⁡(𝐱i)p({\bf x}_{i}), which correspond to maximally sparse areas in the state space, provide the largest contribution to AA. The invariant behavior of the coefficient AA as NbN_{b} increases requires a balance between the decreasing probability weight per single sample and the increasing local probability density.

Consequently, the sensitivity of both AA and α\alpha to the particular quantum state observed in our numerical experiments reflects dimensional compression of the sampled data distribution. This distinguishes our scaling relation from the uncorrelated high-dimensional limits described by Beyer et al. [28], proving that the observed power law is a sensitive descriptor of quantum states expressed through a limited number of measurements.

Below, we examine the intrinsic dimension interpretation through concrete numerical examples, provide a deeper analysis of the measurement data for the quantum state families whose representatives are shown in Fig. 1, and demonstrate possible implementations of our approach.

III Estimating the intrinsic dimension

To systematically validate the direct relation deff=α−1d_{\text{eff}}=\alpha^{-1} revealed in the previous section, we perform controlled numerical benchmarks on synthetic datasets embedded within a high-dimensional hypercube {0,1}N\{0,1\}^{N}. By partitioning the available bits, with total system size NN ranging slightly from 500500 to 504504 bits to ensure exact divisibility, into mm independent and sequentially filled blocks (inset of Fig.2), each generated configuration acts as a coordinate vector on an mm-dimensional manifold. Since each independent axis of length N/mN/m allows for exactly (N/m+1)(N/m+1) sequential binary configurations, the total number of unique accessible states NstatesN_{\text{states}} across the entire manifold is given by Nstates=(Nm+1)mN_{\text{states}}=\left(\frac{N}{m}+1\right)^{m}. For instance, in the case of N=500N=500 and m=10m=10, this restricts the valid configuration space to 5110≈1.19×101751^{10}\approx 1.19\times 10^{17} states, which is fundamentally smaller than the hypercube volume of 25002^{500}. We systematically vary the predefined structural dimension mm from 11 to 1010 and for each mm we randomly generate 10000 samples. The selection of unique outcomes gives NbmaxN_{b}^{\rm max} = 500, 9243, 9986 and 10000 for mm = 1, 2, 3 and m≥4m\geq 4, respectively. Accordingly, to ensure numerical stability, the linear fitting windows for NbN_{b} were strictly selected as [100,400][100,400] for m=1m=1 and [100,9000][100,9000] for m≥2m\geq 2.

If our power-law exponent α\alpha serves as a true indicator of the internal topology, the extracted dimension deff=α−1d_{\text{eff}}=\alpha^{-1} must closely follow the predefined values of mm. Fig. 2 demonstrates that this is indeed the case for m<6m<6, where a good agreement between mm and 1/α1/\alpha is observed. For data of larger dimensions, the deviation of the 1/α1/\alpha value from the true intrinsic dimension increases. This behavior can be attributed to the exponential growth of the available state space with increasing mm, while the number of generated samples remains strictly constant at Nbmax=10000N_{b}^{\rm max}=10000. As the data becomes increasingly sparse within the larger multi-dimensional volume, the scaling of the nearest-neighbor Hamming distance experiences finite-size limitations well-documented in manifold learning literature [28, 27]. Nevertheless, the monotonic trend across the entire m=1​…​10m=1\dots 10 range confirms that the scaling exponent successfully captures the internal structural geometry of the data.

To provide an independent validation of our findings, Fig. 2 also presents the dimensional estimations obtained via the conventional two-nearest-neighbor (TWO-NN) approach [29], which performs well under the assumption that the data density is locally constant. The detailed description of this method is provided in Appendix B. For the TWO-NN analysis, the intrinsic dimension is evaluated using the entire dataset of unique configurations. For m≥2m\geq 2, the resulting dependencies of the intrinsic dimension on the number of unique samples saturate (see Appendix B), demonstrating that the obtained estimation is robust. However, the TWO-NN method fails for m=1m=1 because the distance to the first nearest neighbor and that to the second nearest neighbor are strictly equal for every sample due to the discrete nature of the lattice. Remarkably, for all higher dimensions (m≥2m\geq 2), the TWO-NN curve in Fig. 2 demonstrates a close quantitative agreement with our 1/α1/\alpha scaling framework across the entire tested dimension range.

It is worth mentioning that there is a conceptual difference between the two methodologies for estimating the intrinsic dimension. Our approach operates by fixing the nearest neighbor consideration while systematically expanding the dataset size NbN_{b}, which dynamically compresses the radius of the first Hamming sphere. At the same time, the TWO-NN method relies on multiple fixed spatial scales within a single static dataset by evaluating the ratio of the first and second nearest-neighbor distances (r2/r1r_{2}/r_{1}) [29]. The fact that varying the dataset density at a fixed neighbor index yields equivalent dimensional metrics to varying the neighbor index at a fixed density strictly confirms the scale invariance of the underlying manifold structure.

These findings suggest a much broader application of our nearest-neighbor-based approach for estimating intrinsic dimensions. As an example, in Appendix C we discuss the results obtained for real-world datasets.

IV Distinguishing quantum states

In this section we explain the details of our approach by the example of the Dicke states [30] and then on this basis we will discuss the idea on descriptors of a quantum state. The Dicke wave functions attract considerable attention in quantum computing due to storage [31], networking [32], sensing [33], coding [34] and other applications. These permutationally-invariant quantum states are generally defined as

|ΨND⟩=1CND​∑j𝒫j​(|0⟩⊗N−D⊗|1⟩⊗D).\displaystyle\Ket{\Psi^{D}_{N}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{C^{D}_{N}}}\sum_{j}\mathcal{P}_{j}(\Ket{0}^{\otimes N-D}\otimes\Ket{1}^{\otimes D}). (5)

Here NN is the number of qubits, DD is the parameter that controls the complexity of |ΨND⟩\Ket{\Psi^{D}_{N}} through the number of “1”s in the contributing basis functions, CND=N!/(D!​(N−D)!)C^{D}_{N}=N!/(D!(N-D)!) and the sum goes over all possible permutations of qubits, denoted with 𝒫j\mathcal{P}_{j}. For the given NN the state with D=N/2D=N/2 is characterized by the largest entanglement entropy [6].

Fig. 3(a) presents the r¯1​(Nb)\bar{r}_{1}(N_{b}) functions calculated for the Dicke states of 2424, 6464, and 128128 qubits with different numbers of excitations, specifically D=N/2D=N/2, 3​N/83N/8, and N/4N/4. By choosing these specific wavefunctions, we can probe different degrees of data availability when characterizing quantum states. For instance, for the 2424-qubit Dicke states, a reasonable number of measurements enables the generation of unique bitstrings that almost fully cover the entire available excitation subspace, which is clearly not the case for the 128128-qubit Dicke states. This representative example of the state |D246⟩\ket{D_{24}^{6}}, which possesses the smallest subspace dimension of 134596134596, provides a complete picture of the functional patterns of r¯1\bar{r}_{1} at varying sample sizes NbN_{b}. The initial segment of the function corresponding to Nb∈[10,500]N_{b}\in[10,500] is well approximated by the power law r¯1​(Nb)=8.59​Nb−0.15\bar{r}_{1}(N_{b})=8.59N_{b}^{-0.15}. For Nb>1000N_{b}>1000, the average minimal Hamming distance is characterized by a much faster decay and eventually saturates at the absolute minimal distance of 22 (indicated by the horizontal blue line in Fig. 3(a)) when the sample size reaches Nb=5000N_{b}=5000.

Importantly, the larger the quantum system the more accurate approximation with the power law of the Hamming distance data. In the case of N=64N=64 and 128 we use the range Nb∈[50,1000]N_{b}\in[50,1000] for fitting with Eq. (2). From Fig. 3(b), which provides the power-law parameters for the Dicke states, one can conclude that the analyzed wavefunctions can be successfully discriminated by means of both scaling parameters. For the 1/α1/\alpha quantity, which estimates the effective intrinsic dimension of the measurement datasets, the variation of the values obtained for the Dicke states of the same system size NN is less pronounced than that observed for the coefficient AA. Our results prove that the growth of this inverse scaling exponent with the number of excitations at each NN closely aligns with the trend of the multipartite entanglement entropy established for this family of wavefunctions [6].

Now we are in position to discuss the application of our approach to efficient state discrimination. Traditionally, such a problem is mainly solved through quantum state tomography [35] which is aimed at reconstructing density matrix on a classical computer and becomes unfeasible in the case of the large-scale quantum systems. This motivates developing alternative procedures that are based on descriptors derived from single-qubit measurements across different bases. In this respect, a prominent example is the dissimilarity measure [6] which quantifies the variety of pattern scales present in the bit-string arrays.

Following this idea we propose to use the set of Hamming-distance-based quantities, {A[b],α[b]}\{A^{[b]},\alpha^{[b]}\} calculated in different bases b=1..NBb=1..N_{B} as a distinct geometric descriptor of a quantum state. To demonstrate its practical utility, we compare the half-filled Dicke state, |D2412⟩\ket{D_{24}^{12}}, against a trivial uniform product state, |Ψu⟩=[(|0⟩+|1⟩)/2]⊗24\ket{\Psi_{\rm{u}}}=[(\ket{0}+\ket{1})/\sqrt{2}]^{\otimes 24}, and an entangled Haar-random state, |ΨHaar⟩\ket{\Psi_{\rm{Haar}}}, in a 2424-qubit system. Being strongly delocalized across the computational σz\sigma^{z} basis, these states present a notorious challenge for conventional neural-network quantum state tomography [36, 37] and certification protocols [38].

Fig. 4 illustrates the power-law parameters estimated from measurements in two bases: the standard computational σz\sigma^{z} basis, and a hybrid σx−σz\sigma^{x}-\sigma^{z} basis combining σx\sigma^{x} and σz\sigma^{z} projections for odd and even qubits, respectively. For fitting with Eq. (2) we use the range Nb∈[50,1000]N_{b}\in[50,1000]. Remarkably, while the considered wavefunctions are practically indistinguishable when analyzed solely via σz\sigma^{z} basis measurements, switching to the hybrid σx−σz\sigma^{x}-\sigma^{z} basis enables their highly accurate discrimination. It is worth mentioning that the power-law parameters for the Haar-random states remain nearly invariant with respect to the choice of the measurement basis, yielding AHaarz≈AHaarxzA^{\rm z}_{\rm Haar}\approx A^{\rm xz}_{\rm Haar} and αHaarz≈αHaarxz\alpha^{\rm z}_{\rm Haar}\approx\alpha^{\rm xz}_{\rm Haar}. Additionally, the extracted exponents αxz\alpha^{\rm xz} correspond to effective intrinsic dimensions of deff=7.20d_{\rm eff}=7.20 and 3.663.66 for the Haar-random and uniform states, respectively. This quantitative differentiation perfectly aligns with alternative complexity measures characterizing these multi-body wavefunctions [6].

V Phase boundaries of J1−J2J_{1}-J_{2} model solutions

The possibility of distinguishing quantum states with a limited number of measurements paves the way to a solution of phase classification problem which holds a significant importance in condensed matter physics. To demonstrate this we use a nontrivial example of the two-dimensional J1−J2J_{1}-J_{2} model with antiferromagnetic interactions between nearest (J1J_{1}) and next-nearest (J2J_{2}) neighbours on the N×N\sqrt{N}\times\sqrt{N} square lattice,

HJ1−J2=J1​∑⟨i,j⟩𝐒i​𝐒j+J2​∑⟨⟨i,j⟩⟩𝐒i​𝐒j.\displaystyle H_{J_{1}-J_{2}}=J_{1}\sum_{\braket{i,j}}{\bf S}_{i}{\bf S}_{j}+J_{2}\sum_{\braket{\braket{i,j}}}{\bf S}_{i}{\bf S}_{j}. (6)

Depending on the value of J2J_{2} the model is characterized by phases of different complexity. For instance, the quantum analogs of the classical Néel and stripe phases were found for J2∈[0,0.45]J_{2}\in[0,0.45] and J2∈[0.61,1]J_{2}\in[0.61,1], respectively. Despite considerable efforts, there is still no consensus on the ground states of the J1−J2J_{1}-J_{2} model in the intermediate regime J2∈(0.45,0.61)J_{2}\in(0.45,0.61), which represents a special difficulty for numerical simulations [39]. To find the ground states of the J1−J2J_{1}-J_{2} model on the square lattice with periodic boundary conditions and N=36,64N=36,64 and 100 spins 12\frac{1}{2}, we use the exact diagonalization (ED) [40] and variational neural-network quantum state approach utilizing a Vision Transformer network (ViT) for wave function representation [41, 42] as realized in the NetKet package [43, 44]. The details on the training and sampling procedures are provided in Appendix D.

ED results obtained for the J1−J2J_{1}-J_{2} model on the 6×66\times 6 supercell (the red crosses in Fig.5) evidence that the power α\alpha is sensitive to critical regions of the model phase diagram. In particular, it exhibits a linear behaviour for small J2∈[0,0.3]J_{2}\in[0,0.3] and a smooth maximum spanning the known critical area (J2∈[0.5,0.6]J_{2}\in[0.5,0.6]), with the largest values attained at J2=0.6J_{2}=0.6. The kink observed at this point clearly signals a change in the system’s state and can be attributed to the well-established boundary between intermediate and stripe phases [39]. The demonstrated connection between the exponent α\alpha and intrinsic dimension of the sampling datasets provides an additional confirmation of that similar behaviour of the exponent α\alpha corresponds to the critical behaviour of the system in question. Previous works [12, 16, 45] have revealed that the intrinsic dimension features extrema at the point of equilibrium and non-equilibrium transitions.

These ED results provide a solid basis for analyzing the approximate solutions obtained with the variational ViT quantum state approach. From Fig.5 we observe an excellent agreement between ED and ViT values of the power-law parameter for J2∈[0,0.4]J_{2}\in[0,0.4] (the Néel phase). Expectedly, the largest deviations from the exact solution takes place at the critical J2=0.55J_{2}=0.55 and J2=0.6J_{2}=0.6, which agrees with largest deviations in ground state energies obtained for these points (Appendix D).

Increasing the system size leads to a suppression of the absolute values of the α⁡(J2)\alpha(J_{2}) function. Nevertheless, the variational profiles of the function are robust with the maximum at 0.6. To demonstrate trends more explicitly, we perform a scaling of the ED dependences obtained for the 6×66\times 6 supercell (red dotted lines in Fig.5). For each system size, the scaling factors are defined to match the ViT data at J2=0J_{2}=0. This represents the simplest, non-frustrated regime for simulations, where reliable quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) results [46] are available. The accuracy of our ViT results at J2=0J_{2}=0 can be demonstrated by calculating the relative errors of the ground state energies with respect to the QMC ones (Appendix D). Fig. 5 shows that the ViT power-law parameters (green and blue circles) perfectly match the scaled 6×66\times 6 dependences (red dotted lines) for J2∈(0,0.3]J_{2}\in(0,0.3]. Such agreement may indicate that the ViT provides an accurate approximation of the unknown ground states in this parameter regime. In turn, outside this parameter range (J2>0.3J_{2}>0.3) we observe deviations of the α\alpha values from the scaled curves, which become especially pronounced for the 10×1010\times 10 system. Importantly, at J2=0.5J_{2}=0.5 a pre-trained ViT (pVIT) with 434760 parameters [21] is available for a 10×1010\times 10 system; this model yields a lower ground state energy, EpViT=−0.497508E_{\rm pViT}=-0.497508 than that obtained in our ViT calculations with 155620 parameters, EViT=−0.496783E_{\rm ViT}=-0.496783. Moreover, the deviation of the scaling exponent α\alpha from the rescaled 6×66\times 6 curve (indicated by the purple plus marker in Fig.5) becomes noticeably smaller in comparison with our standard ViT solution. Specifically, the values converge as αpViT=0.06739\alpha_{\rm pViT}=0.06739 and αViT=0.071205\alpha_{\rm ViT}=0.071205 toward the target baseline of αrescaled6×6=0.06594\alpha^{6\times 6}_{\rm rescaled}=0.06594. This quantitative convergence confirms that our geometric metric functions as a sensitive and reliable diagnostic tool for tracking the optimization accuracy of variational quantum states.

Traditionally, the system with J2=0.5J_{2}=0.5 is considered to be the most frustrated one and is used as a benchmark point for different variational eigensolvers [21, 47]. According to our results, the largest deviations from the 6×66\times 6 baseline are observed at J2=0.55J_{2}=0.55 and 0.6, which suggests treating the solutions at these points to be particularly challenging for ViT-based neural quantum state approaches. To confirm these conclusions we have calculated the dimensionless V-score metric [48] that combines the variational energy, EE and energy variance, Var​E=⟨H^2⟩−⟨H^⟩2{\rm Var}E=\braket{\hat{H}^{2}}-\braket{\hat{H}}^{2} estimated for an NN-qubit system. For the J1−J2J_{1}-J_{2} spin model such a metric is given by

V−score=N​Var​EE2,\displaystyle{\rm V-score}=\frac{N{\rm Var}E}{E^{2}}, (7)

and is a reliable estimator for the order of magnitude of the energy relative error [48]. By using V-score, the case of the J1−J2J_{1}-J_{2} square lattice Hamiltonian was identified as a hard problem for variational algorithms where one cannot expect an energy accuracy better than one or two significant digits. Our ViT calculations presented in Fig.5 (b) confirm this for the intermediate values of J2J_{2}. In the regime of zero (J2=0J_{2}=0) or weak (J2∈(0,0.2]J_{2}\in(0,0.2]) frustration, the V-score values are of the order of 10−410^{-4}, which agrees with the previous results [48]. For all the considered systems the V-score functions feature maxima at J2=0.55J_{2}=0.55 on the order of 10−210^{-2}, which correlates with the behaviour of the A⁡(J2)A(J_{2}) function (Appendix D). Thus, the power-law parameters enable us not only to detect phase boundaries, but also to qualitatively characterize the accuracy of the eigenvalue problem solutions.

VI Intrinsic dimension of the quantum annealing data

To demonstrate the versatility of our approach in processing data from different sources, next we analyze the samples obtained in the recent D-Wave quantum annealing experiments [20], where a quantum processing unit (QPU) is programmed to generate samples in close agreement with solutions of the Schrödinger equation for the Ising model Hamiltonian

H(t)=−Γ(t/ta)∑iσix+𝒥(t/ta)∑i​jJi​jσizσjz.\displaystyle H(t)=-\Gamma(t/t_{a})\sum_{i}\sigma^{x}_{i}+\mathcal{J}(t/t_{a})\sum_{ij}J_{ij}\sigma^{z}_{i}\sigma^{z}_{j}. (8)

Here σiμ\sigma^{\mu}_{i} (μ=x,z\mu=x,z) is the Pauli matrix, the couplings Ji​jJ_{ij} are chosen randomly with respect to the different topologies. The time-dependent coefficients Γ⁡(t/ta)\Gamma(t/t_{a}) and 𝒥⁡(t/ta)\mathcal{J}(t/t_{a}) control the Ising and transverse-field contributions in Eq. (8) that have opposite schedules within annealing procedure (Γ⁡(0)>>𝒥⁡(0)\Gamma(0)>>\mathcal{J}(0) at t=0t=0 and Γ⁡(1)<<𝒥⁡(1)\Gamma(1)<<\mathcal{J}(1) at the quench time t=tat=t_{a}).

A system undergoing a quantum phase transition during Schrödinger evolution is described by the quantum Kibble-Zurek mechanism [49, 50, 51], which predicts the formation of the defects due to the finite quench time, tat_{a}. If the Ising part in Eq. (8) described a spin chain with uniform ferromagnetic nearest-neighbor interactions, where the ground state corresponds to collinear ordering, the defects in the measurement results could be easily detected and characterized, as demonstrated in experiments with quantum annealers [52] and Rydberg atom platforms [53]. For the spin glasses, Eq. (8) with random exchange interactions, the situation is more challenging, since the ground-truth states can be found only for small-scale systems (for instance, the 6×66\times 6 square lattice). Fortunately, the spin-glass order parameter ⟨q2⟩\braket{q^{2}} [54] allows quantifying the degree of spin-freezing. Its increase toward unity signifies a reduction in the number of defects and a closer approach to the ideal spin-glass configuration.

In turn, our framework facilitates a better understanding of the configuration space structure and its dynamic evolution with the quench time tat_{a}. Specifically, we analyze experimental data [20] collected for a system with a square lattice topology, as it provides the largest available set of unique bitstrings. The expected minimal Hamming distance functions r¯1​(Nb)\bar{r}_{1}(N_{b}) calculated for the 18×1818\times 18 spin system at different quench times (see Fig. 1) exhibit a well-defined power-law behavior. The scaling rate can be quantitatively evaluated via the exponent α\alpha extracted from the power-law fitting of r¯1​(Nb)\bar{r}_{1}(N_{b}). This power-law scaling holds for smaller models as well (Fig. 6(a)), proving that a longer quench time tat_{a} leads to a stronger localization of the system’s wavefunction within the configuration space. Here, we use Nb∈[50,700]N_{b}\in[50,700] and Nb∈[50,900]N_{b}\in[50,900], depending on the specific number of available unique bitstrings. The extracted exponent is directly linked to the effective intrinsic dimension of the sampling data manifold via deff=α−1d_{\text{eff}}=\alpha^{-1}. As the quench time tat_{a} increases, the steady growth of α\alpha translates into a significant reduction of deffd_{\text{eff}}, capturing how quantum fluctuations compress the delocalized initial state into a compact, low-dimensional subset of target configurations.

To confirm our conclusions regarding the intrinsic dimension behavior in the D-Wave system, we independently evaluate it using the conventional TWO-NN approach [29]. To calculate the dTWO−NNd_{\rm{TWO-NN}} for each system size LL we use a fixed amount of unique bitstrings for all tαt_{\alpha}. Namely, NbN_{b} = 500, 800 and 900 for LL = 8, 10-14 and 18, respectively. The obtained results explicitly highlight the extreme redundancy of the initial NN-dimensional configuration space representation. For instance, at ta=7t_{a}=7 ns, the estimated intrinsic dimension is of the order of the linear system size, dTWO−NN∼Nd_{\rm TWO-NN}\sim\sqrt{N} [Fig.6 (b)]. The obtained results show that dTWO−NNd_{\rm{TWO-NN}} further decreases with tat_{a}, demonstrating that the effective dimensionality of the subspace encompassing the system’s wavefunction outcomes becomes systematically smaller during the annealing process. For all considered datasets, the intrinsic dimension extracted via the TWO-NN method is again in close quantitative agreement with the 1/α1/\alpha scaling framework.

The quench dynamics of small-size spin-glass systems can be accurately reproduced with classical approaches such as the matrix product state (MPS) [20]. We likewise observe excellent agreement between MPS and QPU Hamming-distance quantities characterizing state space [Fig.6] of system with the 8×88\times 8 square lattice. Simulations of larger systems with the same or more complex topologies represent a significant challenge for classical methods. Here, information on state-space properties extracted from experimental data could prove useful for further optimization of classical algorithms. For instance, our results demonstrate a simplification of the wave-function structure with tat_{a}, which motivates the search for more effective classical representations of quantum wave functions with fewer parameters similar to the static case [37, 55, 56, 57, 58].

VII Conclusions

In conclusion, we have revealed a common geometric feature characterizing quantum measurement data obtained from various sources, which manifests as a power-law behavior of the expected minimal Hamming distance between the unique configurations with respect to the number of samples. This robust scaling behavior enables the extraction of inherent data manifold characteristics, such as the power-law parameters AA and α\alpha, independently of the total sample size. We have established the connection between the scaling factor α\alpha and the intrinsic dimension of the sampled data manifold.

On this basis, we have explored a number of critical problems in quantum computing and condensed matter physics, including the efficient discrimination of quantum states, the validation of neural quantum state optimization accuracy, and the structural analysis of quantum annealing experiment outcomes. The introduced Hamming-distance parameters provide direct information on the spatial localization within the configuration space and thus complement standard problem-specific observables, such as magnetic order parameters.

In Appendix C, we extend our scaling analysis onto the real-world classical MNIST dataset to further verify the structural versatility of our geometric approach.

VIII.1 Appendix A: Sample redundancy and linear fitting windows

Bit-string repetitions. Using unique bitstrings is not a restriction of our approach; rather, it is a direct account of the physical reality inherent to the small-size sampling of large-scale quantum systems. The probability of sampling a repetition of any given bitstring decays exponentially with the system size NN. Indeed, for Hilbert spaces of quantum system with N≥30N\geq 30, any computationally feasible measurement record consists entirely of unique configurations by default. In this regime, tracking individual probabilities becomes physically impossible. We explicitly demonstrate this fundamental behavior in Fig.7 using the experimental data from the Google Sycamore processor.

Conversely, retaining repeated bitstrings, if they are present in the measurement dataset, alters the scaling. While the log-log plot remains linear, the straight line exhibits a faster decay, leading to a significantly steeper slope and a higher value of α\alpha. This accelerated power-law behavior occurs because expanding the sample size NbN_{b} leads to a rapid accumulation of identical duplicate configurations separated by zero Hamming distances. As a result, the intrinsic dimension can be severely underestimated. Fig. 8 illustrates this underestimation using the example of 100100-bit synthetic datasets generated for an mm-dimensional manifold by employing the same approach discussed in the main text. In these simulations, we generate 1000010000 bitstrings in total, and the corresponding number of unique outcomes is equal to 100100 (m=1m=1), 24372437 (m=2m=2), 87558755 (m=3m=3), 98629862 (m=4m=4), and 99839983 (m=5m=5). For the m=1m=1 and m=2m=2 cases, where the number of repetitions is the largest and therefore one could approximate the probabilities of individual outcomes, the repetition-based estimates strongly underestimate the true values of mm. At the same time, the repetition-free values of 1/α1/\alpha provide a much better agreement with the predefined intrinsic dimensions.

Selection of fitting ranges. To define the fitting range, we first construct the r¯1​(Nb)\bar{r}_{1}(N_{b}) function in the interval Nb∈[2,Nbmax]N_{b}\in[2,N_{b}^{\text{max}}], where NbmaxN_{b}^{\text{max}} is the number of available unique bitstrings. For all systems considered in our work, we observe a stable linear part of the r¯1​(Nb)\bar{r}_{1}(N_{b}) function in the log-log scale starting at a certain threshold NbminN_{b}^{\text{min}}. To ensure the independence of the resulting parameters AA and α\alpha from the choice of NbminN_{b}^{\text{min}}, we additionally vary it within a local range. The resulting fitting ranges for all the systems under consideration are explicitly specified in the text.

VIII.2 Appendix B: TWO-NN method for estimating intrinsic dimension

The initial dimension of the feature-vectors describing the system in question is usually excessive and the data can be embedded in lower-dimensional space. The dimensionality of such a subspace is called an Intrinsic Dimension [59] and can be associated with the minimal amount of the degrees of freedom and, therefore, with Kolmogorov complexity [60].

In the TWO-NN estimator method [29], the intrinsic dimension is defined with the following equation

dTWO−NN=−ln⁡[1−Femp​(μ)]ln⁡(μ),\displaystyle d_{\rm TWO-NN}=-\frac{\ln[1-F^{\rm emp}(\mu)]}{\ln(\mu)}, (9)

where Femp​(μ)F^{\rm emp}(\mu) is the empirical cumulative distribution function and μ=r2/r1\mu=r_{2}/r_{1} is calculated for each N-dimensional vector from the dataset, where r1r_{1} and r2≥r1r_{2}\geq r_{1} are the distances to the nearest and next-nearest neighbours, respectively. In the initial formulation, Euclidean distance between data points is used. However, nothing, in general, prevents from defining any other relevant metrics depending on the particular task. For instance, in the case of quantum measurements data it is common to use Hamming distance as it is a physically relevant measure [12]. It is important to note, that the TWO-NN algorithm by construction works for datasets of unique samples, since any duplications will immediately lead to the division by zero in μ=r2/r1\mu=r_{2}/r_{1}.

To calculate the dTWO−NNd_{\rm TWO-NN} of the dataset including NbN_{b} bitstrings one needs to sort μ\mu values in the ascending order. After doing this, the empirical cumulative distribution function corresponding to iith bitstring in the sorted dataset can be defined as Femp​(μi)=iNbF^{\rm emp}(\mu_{i})=\frac{i}{N_{b}}. Thus, the resulting points will have coordinates {−ln[1−Femp(μi)],ln(μi)|i=1,…,Nb}\{-\ln[1-F^{\rm emp}(\mu_{i})],\ln(\mu_{i})|i=1,\dots,N_{b}\} and should be fitted with the straight line passing through the origin. The intrinsic dimension is simply the slope of this line (Fig. 9). To make the procedure more robust, we discard the 10% of the points characterized by highest values of μ\mu from the fitting as it was proposed in [29].

To determine the intrinsic dimension of a dataset via the TWO-NN approach, one evaluates it at different sample sizes NbN_{b} and tracks the behavior of the resulting dependence dTWO−NN​(Nb)d_{\rm{TWO-NN}}(N_{b}) [29]. The true intrinsic dimension is defined either as the saturation plateau value or as the value attained at the maximum number of unique samples when saturation is not reached. For instance, for our synthetic datasets with N≈500N\approx 500, the function dTWO−NN​(Nb)d_{\rm{TWO-NN}}(N_{b}) saturates for all dimensions m≥2m\geq 2, as illustrated in Fig. 10(a, b). The opposite behavior is observed for the one-dimensional case with m=1m=1 (see Fig. 10(c)), where the estimated intrinsic dimension initially increases with NbN_{b} and then sharply drops to zero near the maximum number of unique bitstrings. In this case the condition r1=r2r_{1}=r_{2} holds strictly for every sample and the slope of −ln⁡[1−Femp​(μ)]​(ln⁡(μ))-\ln[1-F^{\rm emp}(\mu)](\ln(\mu)) line is zero.

The intrinsic dimension dTWO−NNd_{\rm{TWO-NN}} can be successfully utilized to characterize the structural features of quantum states [12] and serves to identify the most appropriate measurement basis for analyzing specific quantum systems [16]. In some cases, evaluating the intrinsic dimension across different bases even facilitates the detection of quantum phase transitions. In this respect, the dTWO−NNd_{\rm TWO-NN} is closely related to the dissimilarity measure proposed recently by some of us [6]. This quantity was designed to detect phase transitions in quantum systems and is based on the analysis of pattern scales presented in data.

VIII.3 Appendix C: Tests on classical real-world data

In this section, we discuss the potential application of our approach to real-world classical data, using the benchmark MNIST dataset obtained from the Keras Python library [61]. This dataset consists of 70,00070,000 28×2828\times 28 grayscale images of handwritten digits. To calculate r¯1\bar{r}_{1}, r1r_{1} and r2r_{2} between data points in the initial 784-dimensional space we employ the standard Euclidean distance with sample sizes chosen in the range Nb∈[100,6000]N_{b}\in[100,6000]. As can be seen from Fig. 11, 1/α1/\alpha is generally lower than the intrinsic dimension dTWO−NNd_{\rm{TWO-NN}} evaluated at Nb=6000N_{b}=6000 (Fig. 11(b)). However, the hierarchy among the different digit classes remains remarkably consistent in both cases, which demonstrates the feasibility of applying our geometric framework to general datasets of non-quantum origin.

Based on this representative example, one can conclude that using AA, α\alpha and dTWO−NNd_{\rm{TWO-NN}} together may help to distinguish different datasets. According to the results presented in Fig. 11(b), the digits 3 and 8, 6 and 9 as well as 2 and 0 are indistinguishable based only on the dTWO−NNd_{\rm{TWO-NN}} value. At the same time, (see Fig. 11(a)), the classes for digits 6 and 9 lie in different regions with respect to the AA parameter, and the situation for 2’s and 0’s is even better. However, the profiles for 3’s and 8’s still slightly overlap, suggesting that alternative metrics may be required to distinguish these particular datasets. In contrast, the digits 5 and 3 overlap in terms of their α\alpha exponents and lie within the same range of AA, but they remain clearly distinguishable based on their intrinsic dimension dTWO−NNd_{\rm{TWO-NN}}.

Figure 11(c) shows that the power-law behavior of r¯1​(Nb)\bar{r}_{1}(N_{b}) perfectly holds for the MNIST dataset, which supports claims concerning the broad applicability of the proposed approach. Moreover, it paves the way for using the 1/α1/\alpha metric to evaluate the intrinsic dimension of datasets of non-quantum nature based solely on the expected distance to the first nearest neighbor. This is important, for instance, when duplication occurs or there are samples for which several closest neighbors are equally distant. As for the whole MNIST dataset, we obtained 1/α≈12.91/\alpha\approx 12.9 and dTWO−NN≈14d_{\rm TWO-NN}\approx 14 which is in line with previous estimations of the intrinsic dimension d∈[7,15.2]d\in[7,15.2] reported for the different versions of MNIST and various estimation schemes [62, 63]. In our calculations, we used Nb∈[100,10000]N_{b}\in[100,10000] and averaged the results over 50 independent random subsets.

VIII.4 Appendix D: Details of J1−J2J_{1}-J_{2} model calculations

In this section we present technical details concerning calculations of the J1−J2J_{1}-J_{2} models and compare our results with previous works. For small-size systems (36 spins) we use exact diagonalization approach as realized in SpinED package [40]. In turn, for larger systems one needs to employ an approximate scheme, such as variational neural quantum state (NQS) approach. We use the NetKet package realization [43, 44] of an attention-based vision transformer wave function [41, 42], as it is one of the most promising architectures for solving large-scale frustrated magnetic models [64]. For all the system’s sizes we use the same number of the training epochs (1500) and the same ViT architecture that comprises 4 layers, 12 attention heads and embedding dimension of 60, which results in ∼1.5×105\sim 1.5\times 10^{5} trainable parameters. To update the network parameters we use stochastic reconfiguration approach [21] with the built-in MetropolisExchange sampling method. The corresponding number of samples is 4096.

Tables 1 gives the ground state energies obtained for J1−J2J_{1}-J_{2} Hamiltonian defined on supercells of different sizes. In the case of the 6×66\times 6 supercell we compare the ViT energies with the exact diagonalization results. The latter are in full agreement with previous works [65]. The largest deviations between ViT and ED results take place for critical values of J2J_{2} from 0.5 to 0.6. At the same time the best agreement is observed for the Néel phase. As an important benchmark for our non-frustrated results obtained at J2=0J_{2}=0 we consider the Quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) method which provides accurate ground state energies for large-scale systems (up to 96×9696\times 96 spins in [46]). The relative errors of the ViT ground state energies with respect to the QMC ones are approximately equal to 3×10−43\times 10^{-4} % (6×66\times 6 supercell), 8×10−38\times 10^{-3} % (8×88\times 8) and 1×10−21\times 10^{-2} % (10×1010\times 10). For the systems on the 8×88\times 8 and 10×1010\times 10 supercells simulated by using J2>0J_{2}>0 we compare our ViT estimations of the ground state energy with best results (the lowest energies) available in the literature. From Table 1 one can see that for some values of J2J_{2} we obtain a lower energy than known estimates.

Fig. 12 complements Fig.5 presented in the main text and gives the AA parameters from the power-law fitting (Eq. (2)) of the r¯1​(Nb)\bar{r}_{1}(N_{b}) functions calculated for the J1−J2J_{1}-J_{2} model of different sizes. For fitting with power law, Eq. (2) we use the range Nb∈[50,1000]N_{b}\in[50,1000]. The ViT results denoted with color circles features maximum at 0.55, which agrees with the V-score metric.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.
